claim: Heat stress promotes longevity in budding yeast by relaxing the confinement of age-promoting factors in the mother cell.
source: Heat stress promotes longevity in budding yeast by relaxing the confinement of age-promoting factors in the mother cell
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by multiple experimental results including DNA circle propagation assays, barrier measurements, and lifespan analyses.

claim: Upon growth at higher temperature, yeast cells relax the retention of DNA circles, which act as aging factors in the mother cell.
source: We show that upon growth at higher temperature, yeast cells relax the retention of DNA circles, which act as aging factors in the mother cell.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing increased DNA circle propagation frequency at 37°C compared to 30°C.

claim: The enhanced frequency at which circles redistribute to daughter cells was not due to changes of anaphase duration or nuclear shape but solely to the downregulation of the diffusion barrier in the nuclear envelope.
source: The enhanced frequency at which circles redistribute to daughter cells was not due to changes of anaphase duration or nuclear shape but solely to the downregulation of the diffusion barrier in the nuclear envelope.
evidence: Supported by experimental measurements of anaphase duration, nuclear morphology, and barrier strength using FLIP.

claim: The effect of heat stress on DNA circle redistribution depended on the PKA and Tor1 pathways, downstream of stress-response kinase Pkc1.
source: This effect depended on the PKA and Tor1 pathways, downstream of stress-response kinase Pkc1.
evidence: Supported by experiments with constitutively active mutants and pathway inhibitors.

claim: Inhibition of PKA and Tor1 responses restored barrier function and circle retention and abrogated the effect of heat stress on longevity.
source: Inhibition of these responses restored barrier function and circle retention and abrogated the effect of heat stress on longevity.
evidence: Supported by calorie restriction experiments and rapamycin treatment showing restoration of barrier function and lifespan.

claim: Redistribution of aging factors from aged cells to their progeny can be a mechanism for modulating longevity.
source: Our data indicate that redistribution of aging factors from aged cells to their progeny can be a mechanism for modulating longevity.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing correlation between barrier relaxation, DNA circle redistribution, and increased lifespan.

claim: Yeast cells proliferate through budding small, rejuvenated daughter cells from the surface of the larger mother cell.
source: Indeed, these cells proliferate through budding small, rejuvenated daughter cells from the surface of the larger, mother cell (Mortimer and Johnston, 1959; Hartwell and Unger, 1977; Kennedy et al., 1994; Henderson and Gottschling, 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: With each daughter produced, the mother cell ages and progressively loses its division potential until it eventually stops proliferating and dies.
source: Strikingly, with each daughter produced, the mother cell ages and progressively loses its division potential until it eventually stops proliferating and dies.
evidence: This is established knowledge about yeast replicative aging.

claim: The replicative lifespan of haploid wild-type yeast cells reaches about 25 generations on average.
source: This process is called replicative aging and the replicative lifespan, that is, the number of daughters a mother cell generates before dying, is limited, reaching about 25 generations in average for haploid wild-type cells (Henderson and Gottschling, 2008; Denoth Lippuner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Yeast aging manifests through formation of protein aggregates, neutralization of vacuolar pH, fractionation of mitochondrial organization, and decreased sensitivity to signaling pheromone.
source: Beyond limiting the lifespan, yeast aging also manifests itself through a number of additional traits, such as the formation of protein aggregates (Aguilaniu et al., 2003; Erjavec et al., 2007; Hill et al., 2014; Saarikangas and Barral, 2015), the neutralization of the vacuolar pH (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012; Henderson et al., 2014), the fractionation of mitochondrial organization (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012) and the decreased sensitivity of the cell to signaling pheromone (Smeal et al., 1996; Caudron and Barral, 2013; Schlissel et al., 2017) reviewed in Denoth Lippuner et al. (2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Intra-chromosomal recombination between repeated rDNA units excise extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs) that segregate to and accumulate in the mother cell nucleus.
source: Third, intra-chromosomal recombination between repeated rDNA units excise extrachromosomal rDNA circles (ERCs) that segregate to and accumulate in the mother cell nucleus (Szostak and Wu, 1980; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997; Shcheprova et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Old mother cells contain up to thousand ERCs and this load increases exponentially with successive divisions.
source: Old mother cells contain up to thousand ERCs and this load, which increases exponentially with successive divisions, might be what ultimately kills the cell (Sinclair and Guarente, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: High-fidelity retention of DNA circles in the mother cell is facilitated by the formation of lateral diffusion barriers in the ER membrane and the outer nuclear membrane at the bud neck.
source: High-fidelity retention in the mother cell of the DNA circles and of the precursors of protein aggregation is facilitated by the formation of lateral diffusion barriers in the ER membrane and the outer nuclear membrane at the bud neck (Luedeke et al., 2005; Shcheprova et al., 2008; Clay et al., 2014; Saarikangas et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: DNA circles attach to the nuclear envelope through the SAGA complex and nuclear pore complexes (NPCs).
source: DNA circles attach to the nuclear envelope through the SAGA complex and nuclear pore complexes (NPCs) (Shcheprova et al., 2008; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Yeast cells show an extended life span when subjected to mild stresses such as calorie restriction and growth at 37°C.
source: Remarkably, yeast cells show an extended life span when subjected to mild stresses such as calorie restriction and growth at 37°C (Shama et al., 1998a; Shama et al., 1998b; Swieciło et al., 2000; Kapahi et al., 2017).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Similar longevity effects of mild stress take place in organisms as distinct as nematodes, flies and mice.
source: Similar effects take place in organisms as distinct as nematodes, flies and mice, indicating that the regulation of longevity involves similar regulatory pathways in all these organisms, at least upon calorie restriction, namely the TOR and PKA pathways (Steinkraus et al., 2008; Kapahi et al., 2010; Wasko and Kaeberlein, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Mutants affecting the retention of DNA circles in the mother cell are long-lived.
source: Indeed, mutants affecting the retention of DNA circles in the mother cell are long-lived (Shcheprova et al., 2008; Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: In cells grown under optimal conditions (2% glucose, 30°C), DNA circles passed very infrequently to the bud with a propagation frequency of 0.04 ± 0.01.
source: In cells grown under optimal conditions, the circles passed very infrequently to the bud (frequency of propagation to the bud: 0.04 ± 0.01).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Calorie restriction (0.1% glucose, 30°C) had no effect on DNA circle propagation frequency (0.04 ± 0.01).
source: Although calorie restriction had no effect (propagation frequency: 0.04 ± 0.01), the frequency at which individual plasmids passed to the bud was increased four folds in cells grown at 37°C (propagation frequency: 0.17 ± 0.01).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The frequency at which individual DNA circles passed to the bud was increased four-fold in cells grown at 37°C (propagation frequency: 0.17 ± 0.01).
source: Although calorie restriction had no effect (propagation frequency: 0.04 ± 0.01), the frequency at which individual plasmids passed to the bud was increased four folds in cells grown at 37°C (propagation frequency: 0.17 ± 0.01).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The DNA circle propagation frequency in bud6Δ mutant cells is 0.13 ± 0.01.
source: This value is very similar to what we observed in cells lacking the diffusion barrier in the outer nuclear membrane (bud6Δ mutant cells, propagation frequency: 0.13 ± 0.01; Shcheprova et al. (2008); Denoth-Lippuner et al., 2014; Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Increased anaphase duration leaves more time for DNA circles to diffuse from the mother into the bud and therefore promotes their propagation.
source: First, increased anaphase duration leaves more time to circles to diffuse from the mother into the bud and therefore promotes their propagation (Gehlen et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Exposure to heat shortened anaphase duration by about 20% (from 19.7 ± 0.3 to 15.7 ± 0.5 min).
source: Compared to optimal growth conditions, exposure to heat shortened anaphase duration by about 20% (from 19.7 ± 0.3 to 15.7 ± 0.5 min, Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The length of the nucleus was increased in the first 100 seconds of anaphase at 37°C but the scission constriction at the bud neck was unaffected.
source: The length of the nucleus was increased in the first 100 seconds of anaphase but the scission constriction at the bud neck was unaffected (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: DNA circles exchange between mother and bud essentially during early anaphase, with a propagation flux six to eight folds higher in early anaphase than in late anaphase.
source: This frequency was six to eight folds higher in early anaphase than in late anaphase (0.03 ± 0.01 and 0.004 ± 0.003 passage per minute, respectively, Figure 2C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Early anaphase was shorter in cells grown at 37°C compared to 30°C (3.4 ± 0.1 versus 3.9 ± 0.14 min).
source: Remarkably, early anaphase was shorter, certainly not longer, in cells grown at 37°C, compared to 30°C (3.4 ± 0.1 versus 3.9 ± 0.14 min, Figure 2D).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The duration of late anaphase was reduced at 37°C compared to 30°C (12.9 ± 0.46 versus 14.5 ± 0.46 min).
source: The duration of late anaphase was reduced as well (12.9 ± 0.46 versus 14.5 ± 0.46 min, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Early anaphase lasted the longest upon calorie restriction (5.2 ± 0.36 min).
source: Furthermore, early anaphase lasted the longest upon calorie restriction (5.2 ± 0.36 min, Figure 2D), although this condition did not affect the retention of DNA circles (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The correlation between DNA circle and NPC remained intact upon heat shock.
source: Interestingly, the correlation between DNA circle and NPC remained intact upon heat shock.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The increased frequency of circle propagation into the daughter upon growth at higher temperature is not due to circles detachment from NPCs.
source: Thus, the increased frequency of circle propagation into the daughter upon growth at higher temperature is not due to circles detachment from NPCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing maintained NPC-DNA circle correlation at 37°C.

claim: Barrier strength in the nuclear membrane was reduced by roughly half in cells grown at 37°C compared to those grown at 30°C (BI = 24.6 ± 2.5 vs 41.9 ± 4.1).
source: These experiments established that barrier strength in the nuclear membrane was reduced by roughly half in cells grown at 37°C compared to those grown at 30°C (BI = 24.6 ± 2.5 vs 41.9 ± 4.1; Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The barrier index in bud6Δ mutant cells grown at 30°C was similarly decreased (BI = 25.3 ± 3.2).
source: As a positive control, the barrier index in the bud6Δ mutant cells grown at 30°C, which bear strong barrier defects (Shcheprova et al., 2008), was similarly decreased (BI = 25.3 ± 3.2).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The barrier was significantly strengthened in calorie-restricted cells grown in 0.1% glucose (BI = 68.6 ± 15).
source: In contrast, and to our surprise, the barrier was significantly strengthened in calorie-restricted cells grown in 0.1% glucose (BI = 68.6 ± 15, Figure 4D).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The diffusion barrier in the cortical ER was not affected by heat stress and calorie restriction.
source: The diffusion barrier in the cortical ER was not affected by heat stress and calorie restriction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect of temperature and calorie restriction targeted specifically the diffusion barrier in the outer nuclear membrane.
source: Thus, the effect of temperature and calorie restriction targeted specifically the diffusion barrier in the outer nuclear membrane.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing differential effects on nuclear versus cortical ER barriers.

claim: The propagation flux in early anaphase was increased two folds in cells grown at 37°C compared to 30°C (0.06 ± 0.004 versus 0.03 ± 0.01 passage per minute).
source: Indeed, the propagation flux in early anaphase was increased two folds in cells grown at 37°C compared to 30°C (0.06 ± 0.004 versus 0.03 ± 0.01 passage per minute; Figure 4E)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The propagation flux in early anaphase was decreased three folds in calorie restricted cells (0.01 ± 0.01 passage per minute).
source: Indeed, the propagation flux in early anaphase was increased two folds in cells grown at 37°C compared to 30°C (0.06 ± 0.004 versus 0.03 ± 0.01 passage per minute; Figure 4E) and decreased three folds in calorie restricted cells (0.01 ± 0.01 passage per minute).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The propagation flux in bud6Δ mutant cells is 0.10 ± 0.02 passage per minute.
source: The increased propagation flux in heat-stressed cells is comparable to that in the bud6Δ mutant cells (0.10 ± 0.02 passage per minute, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Cells expressing constitutively active PKC1-R398P showed a much weaker barrier compared to wild type cells (BI 19.1 ± 2 versus 41.9 ± 4.1).
source: Supporting the idea that Pkc1 regulates the nuclear barrier, cells expressing this constitutively activated form of Pkc1 showed a much weaker barrier compared to wild type cells (BI 19.1 ± 2 versus 41.9 ± 4.1, Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PKC1-R398P mutation caused a significant reduction in DNA circle retention.
source: Supporting the idea that Pkc1 regulates the nuclear barrier, cells expressing this constitutively activated form of Pkc1 showed a much weaker barrier compared to wild type cells (BI 19.1 ± 2 versus 41.9 ± 4.1, Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and a significant reduction in DNA circle retention (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Constitutive activation of Bck1 using the BCK1-20 allele did not change barrier strength (BI = 38.4 ± 7.1).
source: Constitutive activation of the MAP kinase kinase kinase Bck1, using the BCK1-20 allele, did not change barrier strength (BI = 38.4 ± 7.1, Figure 5B)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Inactivating the MAP kinase Slt2 did not revert the effect of the PKC1-R398P mutation (BI = 17.9 ± 2.1 in the PKC1-R398P slt2∆ double mutant cells).
source: Furthermore, inactivating the MAP kinase Slt2, which acts most downstream in the CWI pathway (Figure 5A), did not revert the effect of the PKC1-R398P mutation (BI = 17.9 ± 2.1 in the PKC1-R398P slt2∆ double mutant cells, Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The slt2Δ mutation by itself tends to slightly weaken the barrier strength (BI = 28.5 ± 4.2).
source: Finally, instead of promoting barrier strength, the slt2Δ mutation by itself tends to slightly weakening the barrier strength (BI = 28.5 ± 4.2), fitting with the cell wall defects observed in these cells.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Activation of the Pkc1 kinase inhibits the diffusion barriers in the nuclear envelope and this effect depends on a distinct signaling branch than the MAP-kinase cascade.
source: Thus, these data indicate that activation of the Pkc1 kinase inhibits the diffusion barriers in the nuclear envelope and that this effect depends on a distinct signaling branch than the MAP-kinase cascade.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing effects of PKC1-R398P but not BCK1-20 or slt2Δ on barrier strength.

claim: Constitutive activation of PKA through deleting BCY1 significantly reduced barrier strength compared to wild type cells (BI = 19.9 ± 1 versus 41.9 ± 4.1).
source: Constitutive activation of PKA through deleting the BCY1 gene that encodes its inhibitory subunit (Toda et al., 1987) significantly reduced barrier strength compared to wild type cells grown in the same conditions (BIn19.9 ± 1 versus 41.9 ± 4.1, Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Expression of the constitutive active allele of Tor1, TOR1-A1957V, reduced barrier strength (BI = 20.75 ± 1.9).
source: Likewise, expression of the constitutive active allele of Tor1, TOR1-A1957V (Reinke et al., 2006) had the same effect (BIn = 20.75 ± 1.9, Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Partial inhibition of Tor1 by addition of rapamycin (200 ng/ml for 16–18 h) increased barrier strength (BI up to 107 ± 24).
source: In reverse, partial inhibition of Tor1 by addition of rapamycin (200 ng/ml for 16–18 h), a TORC1-specific inhibitor, to the growth medium (Brunn et al., 1996; Loewith and Hall, 2011) increased barrier strenght, even more than lowering glucose concentration (BIn up to 107 ± 24 and 68.6 ± 15, respectively Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Calorie restriction abrogated the effect of heat stress on barrier weakening.
source: Whereas cells grown at 37°C in 2% glucose decreased the barrier strength compared to wild-type cells grown in the same medium at 30°C (BI = 24.6 ± 2.5, versus 41.9 ± 4.1, Figure 5E), calorie restriction abrogated this effect.
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Calorie restriction enhanced the barrier in PKC1-R398P mutant cells compared to growth under optimal conditions (BI = 100 ± 40 in 0.1% glucose versus 17.9 ± 2.1 in 2% glucose).
source: Here again, calorie restriction did not simply restore the barrier of the mutant cells, but enhanced it compared to growth under optimal conditions (BI = 100 ± 40 in 0.1% glucose versus 17.9 ± 2.1 in 2% glucose, Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: PKC1-R398P mutant cells grown at 30°C and treated with rapamycin (200 ng/ml) restored the barrier strength to levels similar to those observed in wild-type cells (BI = 42.2 ± 7.7).
source: Interestingly, PKC1-R398P mutant cells grown at 30°C (in 2% glucose) and treated with rapamycin (200 ng/ml), restored the barrier strength to levels similar to those observed in wild-type cells (BI = 42.2 ± 7.7, Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Calorie restriction restored the barrier in bud6Δ mutant cells compared to growth in 2% glucose (BI = 57 ± 9.9 versus 25.3 ± 3.2).
source: Strikingly, calorie restriction also restored the barrier in the bud6Δ mutant cells compared to growth in 2% glucose (BI = 57 ± 9.9 versus 25.3 ± 3.2, respectively; Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplements 1–2).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The strength of the nuclear diffusion barrier is a regulated trait under the control of Tor1 and PKA.
source: Collectively, our data indicate that the strength of the nuclear diffusion barrier is a regulated trait under the control of Tor1 and PKA.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing effects of PKA and Tor1 manipulation on barrier strength.

claim: At 37°C, calorie restriction restored the DNA circle propagation frequency to the levels normally observed at 30°C (0.06 ± 0.01, compared to 0.16 ± 0.02 in 2% glucose).
source: Interestingly, in cells grown at 37°C calorie restriction restored the propagation frequency to the levels normally observed at 30°C (0.06 ± 0.01, compared to 0.16 ± 0.02 in 2% glucose, Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: bud6Δ mutant cells grown at 30°C in 0.1% glucose containing medium retrieved their ability to confine the DNA circle into the mother cell (propagation frequency = 0.04 ± 0.007, compared to 0.12 ± 0.01 in 2%).
source: In line with the reinforcing effect of calorie restriction on the barrier, bud6Δ mutant cells grown at 30°C in 0.1% glucose containing medium also retrieved their ability to confine the DNA circle into the mother cell (propagation frequency = 0.04 ± 0.007, compared to 0.12 ± 0.01 in 2%, Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Restoring barrier strength under heat stress conditions rescues the retention of DNA circles in the mother cell.
source: We conclude that restoring barrier strength under heat stress conditions rescues the retention of DNA circles in the mother cell, indicating that the increased propagation of DNA circles at elevated temperatures (Figure 1C) is indeed caused by a down regulation of the diffusion barrier.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing restoration of circle retention upon barrier restoration.

claim: Cells cultured at 37°C showed 3.3-fold less ERCs than cells cultured at 30°C.
source: While no DNA circles were observed in young cells, a substantial amount could be seen in the old ones. And indeed, cells cultured at 37°C showed 3.3-fold less ERCs than cells cultured at 30°C (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Wild-type cells grown under optimal conditions showed a median lifespan of 23 generations.
source: Whereas wild-type cells grown under optimal conditions showed a median lifespan of 23 generations, calorie restriction increased their median lifespan to 30 generations at 30°C (Figure 7B), as reported (Fontana et al., 2010).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Calorie restriction increased the median lifespan of wild-type cells to 30 generations at 30°C.
source: Whereas wild-type cells grown under optimal conditions showed a median lifespan of 23 generations, calorie restriction increased their median lifespan to 30 generations at 30°C (Figure 7B), as reported (Fontana et al., 2010).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 7B, also supported by citation.

claim: Growth at 37°C increased the longevity to a median lifespan of 32.5 generations.
source: As published (Shama et al., 1998a; Shama et al., 1998b; Swieciło et al., 2000), growth at 37°C increased the longevity to a median lifespan of 32.5 generations (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 7B, also supported by citations.

claim: Calorie restriction of cells grown at 37°C shortened their lifespan back to 27 generations.
source: Calorie restriction of cells grown at 37°C shortened their lifespan back to 27 generations (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: The bud6Δ mutant cells grown at 30°C in rich medium showed an increased lifespan (median lifespan = 39).
source: While the bud6Δ mutant cells grown at 30°C in rich medium showed an increased lifespan (median lifespan = 39), as reported (Shcheprova et al., 2008, Figure 7C)
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 7C, also supported by citation.

claim: Calorie restriction shortened the longevity of bud6Δ mutant cells back to a value close to that of wild type cells under the same conditions (median lifespan = 28.5).
source: While the bud6Δ mutant cells grown at 30°C in rich medium showed an increased lifespan (median lifespan = 39), as reported (Shcheprova et al., 2008, Figure 7C), calorie restriction shortened their longevity back to a value close to that of wild type cells under the same conditions (median lifespan = 28.5; Figure 7C).
evidence: This is directly measured experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Heat stress increases the longevity of the mother cell at least in part through the inhibition of the diffusion barrier in the nuclear envelope and consequently through releasing aging factors to their progeny.
source: This is consistent with the idea that heat stress increases the longevity of the mother cell at least in part through the inhibition of the diffusion barrier in the nuclear envelope and consequently through releasing aging factors, such as DNA circles, to their progeny.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing correlation between barrier inhibition, DNA circle release, and lifespan extension.

claim: Mathematical modeling studies predicted that a retention probability above 99% is required to simulate the aging curves experimentally established for wild type cells.
source: Mathematical modeling studies predicted that a retention probability above 99% is required to simulate the aging curves experimentally established for wild type cells (Gillespie et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The replication origin on the rDNA circles is activated only in about 60% of the cell cycles.
source: This is in part due to the fact that the replication origin on the rDNA circles is activated only in about 60% of the cell cycles (Gillespie et al., 2004)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A slight reduction of retention efficiency has a strong effect on the longevity of the cell.
source: Accordingly, previous studies confirmed that a slight reduction of this retention efficiency has a strong effect on the longevity of the cell (Shcheprova et al., 2008) reviewed in Denoth Lippuner et al. (2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The modulation of barrier strength is not merely a direct consequence of nutrients limitation or temperature increase on barrier formation or stability, but a process elicited by specific regulatory pathways in response to environmental disturbances.
source: Our study establishes that the modulation of barrier strength is not merely a direct consequence of nutrients limitation or temperature increase on barrier formation or stability, but a process elicited by specific regulatory pathways in response to environmental disturbances.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing pathway-specific effects on barrier strength.

claim: Pkc1 might modulate barrier strength through Tor1 and PKA.
source: These data suggest that Pkc1 might modulate barrier strength through Tor1 and PKA.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental data showing pathway interactions.

claim: Heat stress promotes longevity in several species, ranging from flies to worms and rats.
source: Besides S. cerevisiae (Shama et al., 1998a; Shama et al., 1998b; Swieciło et al., 2000), heat stress promotes longevity in several other species, ranging from flies (Smith, 1958; Lithgow et al., 1995; Khazaeli et al., 1997; Le Bourg et al., 2001) to worms (Butov et al., 2001; Cypser and Johnson, 2002; Gems and Partridge, 2008; Rodriguez et al., 2012) and rats (Holloszy and Smith, 1986).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: Prokaryotic and eukaryotic species exposed to elevated temperatures induce the expression of heat shock proteins (HSPs) that are well conserved among species and help the cell maintain proteostasis.
source: Heat stress is also a protein denaturant agent. Prokaryotic and eukaryotic species exposed to elevated temperatures induce the expression of heat shock proteins (HSPs) that are well conserved among species and help the cell maintain proteostasis (Lindquist and Craig, 1988; Morano et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The lifespan extension observed in S. cerevisiae upon heat stress requires the heat shock protein Hsp104.
source: Additionally, the lifespan extension observed in S. cerevisiae upon heat stress, requires the heat shock protein Hsp104 (Shama et al., 1998a; Shama et al., 1998b).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HSPs expression decreases with ageing in mammals, flies and worms.
source: HSPs expression decreases with ageing in mammals, flies and worms (Kurapati et al., 2000; Wyttenbach et al., 2002; Hsu et al., 2003)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: HSPs expression positively correlates with maximum longevity in mammals and birds.
source: HSPs expression decreases with ageing in mammals, flies and worms (Kurapati et al., 2000; Wyttenbach et al., 2002; Hsu et al., 2003) and positively correlates with maximum longevity in mammals and birds (Salway et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: A potent mechanism to promote longevity is the opening of the diffusion barrier in the nuclear envelope and the 'dumping' of at least some of the mother's burden onto their daughters.
source: In striking contrast, we show here that a potent mechanism to promote longevity is the opening of the diffusion barrier in the nuclear envelope and the 'dumping' of at least some of the mother's burden onto their daughters.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing barrier opening and its effects on longevity.

claim: Barrier weakening is not the only mechanism through which cells can modulate the effects of age.
source: Barrier weakening is clearly not the mechanism promoting longevity in response to calorie restriction, establishing that it is not the only mechanism through which cells can modulate the effects of age.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing different mechanisms for different stresses.

claim: The fact that rescuing DNA circle confinement largely abolishes the effect of heat stress on lifespan extension indicates that 'dumping' age load onto the population is a prominent mechanism of longevity regulation under heat stress.
source: In any case, the fact that rescuing DNA circle confinement largely abolishes the effect of heat stress on lifespan extension indicates that at least under that condition 'dumping' age load onto the population is a prominent mechanism of longevity regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing restoration of circle confinement abolishing lifespan extension.

claim: Other aging factors, such as deposit precursors, also depend on the diffusion barrier for their confinement in the mother cell.
source: However, the fact that other factors, such as deposit precursors (Saarikangas et al., 2017) also depend on the diffusion barrier for their confinement in the mother cell suggest that the regulation we have uncovered might affect more than only DNA circles.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: The regulation of barrier permeability might affect more than only DNA circles.
source: However, the fact that other factors, such as deposit precursors (Saarikangas et al., 2017) also depend on the diffusion barrier for their confinement in the mother cell suggest that the regulation we have uncovered might affect more than only DNA circles.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on known dependencies of other factors on the barrier.

claim: Calorie restriction extends the replicative lifespan of yeast cells without affecting circle confinement.
source: In addition, the fact that calorie restriction extends the replicative lifespan of yeast cells without affecting circle confinement indicates that barrier opening is not the only mechanism of longevity modulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing lifespan extension without changes in circle confinement.

claim: Middle-age mother cells cope better with heat than young ones.
source: Remarkably, middle-age mother cells do cope better with heat than young ones (reviewed in Denoth Lippuner et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Around 30% of the genome can recombine out of the chromosomes and form DNA circles.
source: In favor of such a model, it has been recently shown that around 30% of the genome can recombine out of the chromosomes and form DNA circles (Møller et al., 2015).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Some DNA circles carry genes likely to promote survival in response to specific stresses, such as cupper intoxication and salt stress.
